Chapter 8

Technical Principles and Strategy

技术原则与技术战略

The phrase “developing and implementing technical principles and strategies” sounds fancy—like the title of a 200-slide deck that someone with “enterprise architect” in their job title puts together. In reality, it’s just a fancy way of saying, “What do our technology, principles, architecture, and capabilities need to look like, and how do we get them there to meet our business goals?”

“制定并落地技术原则与技术战略”——这个说法听上去很唬人，就像那种头衔里带“企业架构师”的人会做出来的 200 页幻灯片标题。实际上，它不过是把一句大白话包装了一下：“我们的技术、原则、架构和能力应该长成什么样？又该如何把它们弄到那个状态，来支撑我们的业务目标？”

More formally, technical strategy is the comprehensive plan that aligns technology decisions, architecture choices, and capability development with business objectives, providing a framework for making consistent technical decisions that support organizational goals.

更正式地说，技术战略（technical strategy）是一套综合性规划：它把技术决策、架构选型和能力建设与业务目标对齐，为做出前后一致、并能支撑组织目标的技术决策提供一个框架。

Technical principles and strategy (from here on, we’ll just say “strategy”) are part of a roadmap—and indeed, they should be included in your current roadmap. The product features that you plan to build must be supported by the technology and architecture underpinning them. If you’re planning a significant new feature that needs more scale, then your technical strategy must address how that scale will be achieved. It’s also a blueprint—though in many chaotic organizations, it’s one that’s frequently updated and revised. Part architecture document, part register of tools and their selection criteria and evolution, it provides the foundation for planning the addition of people and specific skill sets to your team.

技术原则与技术战略（下文我们就简称“战略”）是路线图的一部分——而且确实应该被纳入你当前的路线图。你计划做的产品功能，必须有底层的技术与架构来支撑。如果你在规划一个需要更大规模的重要新功能，那么技术战略就必须回答：这个规模要怎么实现。它同时也是一张蓝图——只不过在许多混乱的组织里，这张蓝图需要频繁更新修订。它一半是架构文档，一半是工具台账（含选型标准与演进轨迹），并为你规划“给团队补充哪些人、哪些技能”提供基础。

In this chapter, we explore the core principles, frameworks, and practices that underpin technical strategies. We’ll give you a practical look at how to use technical strategy to tackle pesky challenges, like thinking about what’s next and how to get there, dealing with legacy systems nobody wants to touch, or ensuring you’re constantly evaluating what works and what doesn’t. This is a practical guide for teams living in worlds where the only thing you can count on is that everything will change tomorrow.

本章我们会探讨支撑技术战略的核心原则、框架与实践，并带你实际看一看：如何用技术战略去对付那些烦人的难题——比如想清楚下一步是什么、怎么走到那里，处理没人愿意碰的遗留系统，或者持续评估哪些做法有效、哪些无效。这是一本给这类团队的实操指南：他们身处的世界里，唯一能指望的事情就是“明天一切都会变”。

Why Does Technical Strategy Matter?

技术战略为什么重要？

Let’s face it: a well-thought-out technical strategy is crucial if you want your organization to grow without imploding. Your technical strategy ensures that all those technical and engineering decisions—from big-picture architecture stuff down to “Which JavaScript framework should we use this week?”—align with what your company is trying to accomplish. This alignment isn’t just nice to have; it ensures that every tech investment and process tweak is helping you meet your business goals. In other words, you develop your technical strategy by weaving it into your organization’s game plan, connecting your tech choices with what you’re trying to achieve in the market.

实话实说：如果你想让组织在增长的同时不把自己撑爆，一套深思熟虑的技术战略至关重要。技术战略保证了所有技术与工程决策——从宏观架构一路到“这周我们该用哪个 JavaScript 框架”——都与公司想达成的目标对齐。这种对齐不是可有可无的点缀，它确保每一笔技术投入、每一次流程微调都在帮你靠近业务目标。换句话说，技术战略是织进组织整体作战计划里的，它把你的技术选择和你想在市场上达成的东西连在一起。

In today’s world and in most, if not all, chaotic environments, any rigid plan will be obsolete before you finish your morning coffee. Technical strategies need to be flexible and iterative. With a flexible approach, you can move people and shift priorities without significantly disrupting ongoing projects. There’s always a balance that needs to be struck between being able to move quickly and avoiding flailing.

在当今世界、以及绝大多数（如果不是全部）混乱环境里，任何刚性计划往往在你喝完早咖啡之前就已经过时了。技术战略必须灵活、可迭代。有了灵活的姿态，你就可以调动人员、调整优先级，而不至于严重冲击正在进行的项目。在“快速行动”和“避免乱扑腾”之间，永远需要拿捏好分寸。

Remember that strategy is more than what widgets we should buy or build; nonfunctional needs, like security, compliance, and availability, must be addressed by your strategy. For a lot of chaotic organizations, we see two modes for nonfunctional needs: we ignore them or we overcompensate for them.

记住：战略不只是“该买还是该造哪个组件”；安全、合规、可用性这类非功能性需求（nonfunctional needs）也必须由你的战略来回答。在很多混乱组织里，我们看到对非功能需求只有两种模式：要么无视，要么过度补偿。

A technical strategy means asking yourself important questions. For example, what do you need for security, compliance, or availability? Review whether you have customers in the European Union, meaning General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) must be considered. Or do most of your customers expect you to have Systems and Organization Controls 2 (SOC2) compliance standards in place? Do you need two cloud regions or enhanced availability because you’ve promised customers a specific uptime? Perhaps those seem like reasonable investments that address real needs, which you can probably afford without breaking the budget and constraining your ability to iterate and ship software. Your risks and constraints may differ in larger organizations, and your strategy should reflect that. A solid technical strategy is a good place to document your thoughts about today’s needs and avoid premature optimization.

技术战略意味着你要问自己一些重要的问题。比如：安全、合规、可用性方面你需要什么？看看你是否有欧盟客户——如果有，就必须考虑《通用数据保护条例》（GDPR）。又或者，你的大多数客户是否期望你已经通过了 SOC2（系统与组织控制 2 类）合规？因为向客户承诺了某个具体的可用率，你是否需要双云 region 或更高的可用性？这些看起来可能都是针对真实需求的合理投入，而且你大概负担得起，既不会击穿预算，也不会束缚自己迭代和交付软件的能力。在更大的组织里，你的风险与约束会不一样，战略也应当反映这一点。一套扎实的技术战略，正是用来记录你对当下需求的思考、并避免过早优化的好地方。

Another important piece is ensuring your technical and product strategies play nicely together. In early-stage companies, these are often inseparable; your technical choices directly enable or constrain your product capabilities. As organizations mature, product and technical strategies may diverge but must remain aligned. While product strategy focuses on what needs to be built and why you’re building it, technical strategy provides the framework for how you will build those products. You’ll need both to build products that meet business goals even when everything around you changes at warp speed.

另一个要点是：要确保技术战略与产品战略能友好共处。在早期公司，这两者往往不可分——你的技术选择直接决定了产品能力能做到什么、又受什么限制。随着组织成熟，产品战略与技术战略可能会分叉，但必须保持对齐。产品战略关注“要造什么、为什么造”，技术战略则提供“你要怎么造”的框架。即便周遭一切都在以曲速变化，你也需要这两者合力，才能造出符合业务目标的产品。

Building a Foundation

打好地基

You must know where you stand before you can aim for the stars. Understanding your organization’s current landscape is an essential starting point for any technical strategy. That journey starts with putting together an inventory. It’d be wonderful if this inventory contained detailed systems documentation, equipment inventories, network configuration diagrams, and the policies and procedures governing their use. (We know; we think that’s funny too.) It’s far more likely your journey will start with a list of applications, languages, frameworks, and tools. Your mission is to evolve that inventory into (more) mature documentation. Indeed, far from being some static record gathering dust on a shelf, this inventory is the baseline for every architectural decision and technology investment.

在仰望星空之前，你得先知道自己站在哪儿。理解组织当前的格局，是任何技术战略不可或缺的起点。这段旅程始于盘家底。如果这份家底清单里已经有详尽的系统文档、设备台账、网络配置图，以及管着它们的政策与流程，那当然再好不过。（我们知道，我们也觉得这画面挺可笑的。）更可能的情况是：你的旅程起点只是一份应用、语言、框架和工具的列表。你的任务就是把这份清单逐步演进成（更）成熟的文档。说到底，这份家底绝不是落灰的静态档案，而是每一个架构决策、每一笔技术投入的基线。

Based on his initial conversations with the team, Figure 8-1 is the initial systems architecture diagram that James created on his first day at a startup in the past.

图 8-1 是 James 当年在一家初创公司入职第一天，基于和团队的初步交谈画出来的初始系统架构图。

— 原书第 169 页 —

It’s not rocket science, overly time consuming, or complicated. It’s an attempt to outline the architecture, some of the workflow, and key tools that are essential to the environment. By the end of the first week, James had done the following:

这不是什么火箭科学，既不耗时也不复杂。它只是试图勾勒出架构、一部分工作流，以及该环境里必不可少的关键工具。到第一周结束时，James 已经做了如下这些事：

  • Drawn all over this diagram to add notes, and added more workflows

    在这张图上到处画线加备注，并补充了更多工作流

  • Documented all (most) of the other tools being used and identified any tooling gaps

    把正在使用的其他工具全部（大部分）文档化，并识别出工具缺口

  • Identified single points of failure

    识别出单点故障

  • Matched systems and tools to internal owners and experts (e.g., Rae as the expert on the backend, Jeff as the subject matter expert on the React frontend, and Jess managing the CI/CD workflow)

    把系统和工具对应到内部的负责人与专家（例如 Rae 是后端专家、Jeff 是 React 前端的主题专家、Jess 负责 CI/CD 工作流）

  • Started to discuss the strengths and weaknesses of specific subsystems (e.g., less than 50% test coverage for the backend)

    开始讨论具体子系统的优劣（例如后端测试覆盖率不足 50%）

  • Worked out if there were any documentations, procedures, or policies for the operation of the environment (spoiler: there was not a great deal)

    搞清楚该环境的运维是否有文档、流程或政策（剧透：没多少）

  • Worked out where they stood on nonfunctional requirements like security and compliance

    搞清楚他们在安全、合规等非功能需求上处于什么位置

  • Started organizing this information into a structure, identifying gaps in his knowledge, and formulating a strategy for what to tackle first

    开始把这些信息组织成结构，识别自己知识上的空白，并制定“先啃哪一块”的策略

With a clear(-ish) picture of your existing systems, you can assess capabilities, identify gaps, and prioritize what needs to be done. For example, understanding your current application, network architecture, and system dependencies helps pinpoint bottlenecks or single points of failure that might make scalability a nightmare. Similarly, having some idea of how things work—even if it’s just rough flowcharts and diagrams rather than well-documented policies and procedures—ensures that changes or upgrades are more likely to be smooth and, sometimes, more likely to be feasible. This reduces the risk of things going wrong and paves the way for smooth improvements.

对现有系统有了一幅（还算清楚的）图景之后，你就能评估能力、找出缺口，并给该做的事排优先级。例如，了解当前的应用、网络架构和系统依赖，能帮你精准定位那些可能让可扩展性变成噩梦的瓶颈或单点故障。同样，对“事情是怎么运转的”有个大致概念——哪怕只是粗糙的流程图和示意图，而不是完备的政策与流程文档——也能让变更或升级更可能平稳落地、有时甚至让原本不可行的事情变得可行。这降低了出问题的风险，为顺利改进铺平道路。

You Need More than Technical Widgets

你需要的不只是技术零件

The technical inventory is just one piece of the puzzle. Leaders also need to understand the human and process-related dimensions of their current systems. This need means understanding team expertise, current workflows, and how various people, processes, and components depend on each other. Ultimately, technical strategies are implemented, and the results are operated by the humans who work with you. You need to understand how things work now and who does them, and then ensure that whatever you introduce in your technical strategy can be implemented and operated. The most brilliant technical strategy in the world that your team can’t execute is just a nice but useless artifact.

技术家底只是拼图的一块。领导者还需要理解现有系统在“人”和“流程”维度的情况。这意味着要理解团队的专长、当前的工作流，以及各色人、流程和组件之间如何互相依赖。归根到底，技术战略是要靠和你一起共事的人去落地、去运营的。你必须先搞清楚现在事情是怎么运转的、谁在做，然后确保你在技术战略里提出的任何东西都能被执行、被运营。世界上最聪明的技术战略，如果团队执行不了，也只是一件好看但没用的摆件。

Some years ago, James created Figure 8-2, a mind map of the areas he asked about when he started at a new organization. Some of them are more relevant than others, depending on your role and the scale of your organization. They aren’t a definitive list of areas to explore, but they provide a good starting point.

几年前，James 画了图 8-2 这样一张思维导图：它罗列了他到一个新组织上任时会去了解的各个领域。其中哪些更相关，取决于你的角色和组织规模。它不是一份“必须探索的领域”的权威清单，但提供了一个不错的起点。

While the mind map James created covers four major domains (company, product, technical, and humans), the deep dive in this book on technical strategy focuses primarily on the technical domain. Earlier chapters cover the organizational, product, and human aspects in detail. Here, we’ll assume you’ve done that groundwork and can now focus on the technical strategy itself.

James 这张思维导图覆盖了四大领域（公司、产品、技术、人），但本书对技术战略的深入探讨主要聚焦在技术域。组织、产品和人这些方面，前面的章节已经详细讲过。这里我们假设你已经打好了那些底子，可以专注于技术战略本身了。

Not every item on the map is relevant to every organization, at least not at every stage of evolution. Instead, it serves as a helpful mental checklist. We recommend skimming through most of the items and reaching one of three conclusions in relation to your organization:

图上的每一项并非对每个组织都适用，至少不是在每个发展阶段都适用。它更像一份有用的心智清单。我们建议你大致过一遍这些条目，并就你的组织得出三种结论之一：

  1. No action is needed; everything is going smoothly.

    不需要行动；一切运转顺利。

  2. This needs work; let’s determine what to do and when.

    这块需要改进；让我们定一下做什么、什么时候做。

  3. There’s nothing here, and should that worry me?

    这里什么都没有，我是不是该为此担心？

You can then determine what’s broken, prioritize what needs to be fixed, and watch for emerging issues. You then combine this understanding with your technical insights into a foundational view of how things look now. With this, assuming you don’t resign in horror, you can work toward a strategy for tackling the key items.

由此你就能判断哪里坏了、给该修的东西排优先级，并留意正在冒头的问题。再把这份理解与你的技术洞察合在一起，形成一幅“现在局面如何”的基础视图。有了它——前提是你没被吓得当场辞职——你就可以朝着“先啃哪些关键项”的策略推进了。

Establishing Technical Principles

确立技术原则

At the heart of every effective technical strategy are technical principles. We use these principles to guide all our strategy’s engineering decisions. The best technical principles are clear, concise, and easy for everyone in the organization to understand—whether you’re a seasoned engineer or the new hire who started last Monday. They ditch complex jargon in favor of language that makes sense to both technical and nontechnical stakeholders.

每一套有效技术战略的核心，都是技术原则（technical principles）。我们用这些原则来指导战略中的一切工程决策。最好的技术原则清晰、凝练，组织里的每个人都能轻松理解——无论你是资深工程师，还是上周一刚入职的新人。它们抛弃复杂行话，改用技术与非技术干系人都能听懂的语言。

A key characteristic of practical technical principles is that they’re forward looking and aspirational. They must be robust enough to support long-term growth while still adapting to your organization’s evolving needs. In practical terms, while the principles must be specific enough to guide everyday decision making, they must also be flexible enough to accommodate new ideas. We’ve discussed how chasing new shiny things can be dangerous and counterproductive, but sometimes change makes sense. If your technical principles restrict thinking about innovation and evolution, your team will bypass or ignore them. For instance, principles that emphasize modularity and loose coupling in software design not only streamline current development efforts but also make it way easier to integrate new technologies as they become available.

实用的技术原则有一个关键特征：面向未来、带有愿景色彩。它们既要足够稳健，能支撑长期增长，又要能适应组织不断变化的需求。落到实操上，原则既要具体到能指导日常决策，又要灵活到能容纳新想法。我们讨论过追逐新鲜玩意儿多么危险、多么适得其反，但有时候改变是合理的。如果你的技术原则把对创新与演进的思考都堵死了，团队就会绕过它、无视它。举例来说，在软件设计中强调模块化与松耦合的原则，不仅能简化当前的开发工作，也会让未来新技术出现时的接入变得容易得多。

Your technical principles are also likely to be aspirational. Some principles may be reflected in you, your team, and your environment. Alternatively, you may have parts of your organization where what you’ve built aligns with the ideal expressed by your principles. But much of your environment is often a cautionary tale of what happens when you don’t follow technical principles. So, does this mean technical principles are empty words? Absolutely not—technical principles have a powerful two-fold function in this instance.

你的技术原则往往也带有愿景色彩。有些原则可能已经体现在你、你的团队和你的环境里；或者，组织中可能有一部分所构建的东西已经贴合原则所表达的理想。但你所处环境的大部分，往往是一个“不遵循技术原则会怎样”的警示故事。那么，这是不是说技术原则只是空话？绝对不是——在这种情形下，技术原则有着强大的双重功能。

— 原书第 173 页 —

First, they stop you from making things worse. It’s easy to throw good money after bad, but if you use your technical principles as a compass, then they will help you avoid making a worse decision on top of a bad situation. They give you an aspirational target and define what good looks like, so you know where you need to aim when developing your strategy and when implementing that strategy.

第一，它们阻止你把事情搞得更糟。雪上加霜、把好钱扔在坏钱后面，是很容易的事；但如果你把技术原则当作罗盘，它们就能帮你避免——在已经很糟的局面上——再做一个更糟的决定。它们给你一个有愿景的目标，定义了“好”长什么样，让你在制定战略和落地战略时都清楚该瞄准哪里。

Second, the (massive) bonus prize you also get from technical principles is that they don’t just guide your strategy; they are reference points that help you make good decisions throughout your product and development lifecycle. They live beyond your strategy, with the best technical principles being the ones that you reference when you review a pull request, read a product design, or examine a new technology. You can also go back into creating your technical principles by bubbling up the principles that your team thinks make good software and culture. We go into this in more depth in Chapter 9, where technical principles also help us make good changes.

第二，技术原则还给你一份（超大额）彩蛋奖励：它们不只指导你的战略，还是你在整个产品与开发生命周期中做出好决策的参照点。它们的寿命超出战略本身——最好的技术原则，是你在评审一个 Pull Request、读一份产品设计、或考察一项新技术时都会去翻出来对照的那些。你还可以反过来，把团队心目中“什么造就好软件、好文化”的原则提炼上来，反哺技术原则的制定。这一点我们会在第 9 章深入展开——在那里，技术原则还能帮我们做出好的变更。

Example Technical Principles

技术原则示例

So, what technical principles should you have? It’s hard to create a comprehensive list for every organization at every stage of evolution. But this section outlines an example list of 14 practical principles that a software engineering team might want to adopt.

那么，你应该有哪些技术原则？要为每个发展阶段的每个组织都列一份完备清单很难。但本节给出了一份 14 条实用原则的示例清单，供软件工程团队参考采纳。

These principles represent both aspirational goals and practical trade-offs. Early-stage teams might adopt fewer principles with more flexibility, while mature organizations might enforce stricter adherence. Each principle directly supports business goals by either reducing costs (through maintainability and automation), increasing customer satisfaction (through reliability and performance), or enabling growth (through scalability and modularity):

这些原则既代表愿景目标，也代表现实权衡。早期团队可以采用更少、更灵活的原则；成熟组织则可以要求更严格地遵守。每条原则都直接支撑业务目标——要么通过可维护性与自动化降低成本，要么通过可靠性与性能提升客户满意度，要么通过可扩展性与模块化支持增长：

Simplicity first. Prefer straightforward, clear solutions over complex ones. This reduces support costs and accelerates onboarding.

简洁优先。优先选择直接、清晰的方案，而不是复杂的方案。这能降低支持成本、加速新人上手。

Scalability. Design systems that can scale horizontally and vertically. This enables customer growth without architecture rewrites.

可扩展性。设计能够横向与纵向扩展的系统。这让客户增长时不必重写架构。

Modularity. Build your systems in independent, interchangeable components. This enables parallel development and reduces time to market.

模块化。用独立、可互换的组件来构建系统。这支持并行开发、缩短上市时间。

Reliability. Prioritize fault tolerance and resilience in your designs. This increases customer retention and reduces churn.

可靠性。在设计中优先考虑容错与韧性。这能提高客户留存、降低流失。

— 原书第 174 页 —

Maintainability. Write code that is easy to understand, modify, and debug, and ensure consistency through standards, automation, and validation. This will reduce long-term costs.

可维护性。写出易于理解、修改和调试的代码，并通过标准、自动化与校验来保证一致性。这会降低长期成本。

Documentation. Treat documentation as integral, not optional. This accelerates onboarding and reduces knowledge silos.

文档化。把文档视为不可或缺的一部分，而非可选项。这能加速新人上手、减少知识孤岛。

Testing. No untested code will be merged and no code that fails tests will be merged. This rule reduces defects and improves customer satisfaction.

测试。未测试的代码不得合入，测试不通过的代码不得合入。这条规则减少缺陷、提升客户满意度。

Visibility. Observability and metrics are core requirements, not afterthoughts. This principle enables data-driven decisions.

可观测性。可观测性与指标是核心需求，不是事后补的功课。这条原则让数据驱动决策成为可能。

Security by design. Incorporate security considerations at every stage. To reduce breach risks and maintain customer trust, security must not be an afterthought.

安全左移（安全内建）。在每个阶段都纳入安全考量。为降低被攻破的风险、维护客户信任，安全绝不能事后再补。

Performance awareness. Balance optimization efforts with practical requirements to improve user experience.

性能意识。在优化投入与实际需求之间取得平衡，以改善用户体验。

Consistency. Use established patterns and standards consistently. This reduces cognitive load and speeds up development.

一致性。一致地使用既定模式与标准。这降低认知负荷、加快开发。

Automation. Automate repetitive tasks whenever possible to reduce operational costs.

自动化。尽可能把重复任务自动化，以降低运维成本。

Openness. Design for interoperability and openness, using open standards. This avoids vendor lock-in.

开放性。面向互操作性与开放性设计，使用开放标准。这避免厂商锁定。

Evolution. Architect systems anticipating change and evolution. This reduces future refactoring costs.

演进性。在架构设计中预留变化与演进的空间。这降低未来重构的成本。

Many of these principles will resonate with you and your team. Indeed, we recommend using these examples as a starting point for discussing technical principles. But building your technical principles should be a collaborative effort—created by and living inside your team.

这些原则中，很多会让你和团队产生共鸣。确实，我们建议以这些示例为起点，去讨论你们自己的技术原则。但构建技术原则应当是一项协作成果——由团队共创、并活在团队之中。

— 原书第 175 页 —

Crafting Technical Principles Workshop

技术原则工作坊

Let’s walk through a practical workshop format that we’ve found effective for teams developing their technical principles. This structured approach helps ensure that your principles emerge from collective wisdom rather than individual preference.

下面带大家过一遍一套实操工作坊流程——我们发现它对团队打磨自己的技术原则很有效。这种结构化方式能确保你们的原则来自集体智慧，而不是某个人的偏好。

Exercise: Crafting Technical Principles for Startups

练习：为初创企业打磨技术原则

Objective. The goal is to collaborate and develop technical principles that will guide a startup engineering team in making effective, aligned decisions as the startup grows.

目标。通过协作打磨出一套技术原则，在初创公司成长过程中，指导其工程团队做出有效、彼此对齐的决策。

Materials Needed. An online collaborative whiteboard tool (such as Miro, Mural, or FigJam); a timer to keep the workshop focused and energetic (Note that the suggested times are just that—suggested. If you have a larger or smaller team, you can adjust them.)

所需材料。一个在线协作白板工具（如 Miro、Mural 或 FigJam）；一个计时器，让工作坊保持专注和活力（注意：建议时长只是建议，团队更大或更小都可以调整）。

Preparation. Before starting, ensure everyone understands why technical principles matter (i.e., they serve as decision-making guardrails that align the team and provide consistency over time).

准备。开始之前，确保每个人都理解技术原则为什么重要（也就是说，它们充当决策护栏，让团队对齐，并在时间长河中保持一致性）。

Exercise Steps.

练习步骤。

Step 1: Idea dump (10 minutes). Have each team member use the online collaborative board to post their ideas for principles as individual sticky notes. Encourage everyone to think broadly. What values should guide technical decisions? What have they learned from past experiences? This is a judgment-free brainstorming phase, so quantity matters more than quality at this stage.

第 1 步：想法倾倒（10 分钟）。让每位团队成员在在线协作白板上，把自己对原则的想法写成一张张便利贴。鼓励大家放开思路：哪些价值观应当指导技术决策？他们从过去的经历中学到了什么？这是一个不评判的头脑风暴阶段，此阶段数量比质量更重要。

Step 2: Grouping and naming (10 minutes). As a group, start categorizing the posted principles into themes. Each theme could then be summed up with an overarching principle. For example, sticky notes like “Prioritize scalability” and “Optimize for performance” might fall under a broader category, such as “Build for growth.” This consolidation helps identify patterns in the team’s thinking and reduces overlapping concepts.

第 2 步：分组与命名（10 分钟）。作为一个整体，把贴出来的原则归类成若干主题。每个主题再用一条总括性原则来收束。例如“优先考虑可扩展性”和“为性能优化”这类便利贴，可以归到一个更大的类别下，比如“为增长而建”。这种合并有助于识别团队思考中的模式、减少概念重叠。

Step 3: Voting (5 minutes). Give each participant three votes to place on the principles or themes they find most crucial. Votes can be distributed however individuals choose—all on one principle or spread across multiple. This democratic approach ensures the final principles reflect the collective priorities of the team.

第 3 步：投票（5 分钟）。给每位参与者三票，投给他们认为最关键的原则或主题。投票怎么分配由个人决定——全押在一条原则上，或分散在多条上都行。这种民主方式能确保最终的原则反映团队的集体优先级。

— 原书第 176 页 —

Step 4: Drafting principles (15 minutes). Break into smaller groups or stay as one team (depending on the size of your group) to draft well-articulated versions of the top-ranked principles. For each principle, define what it means, why it’s essential, and provide a concrete example to make it tangible. The goal is to transform general ideas into actionable guidance that can inform day-to-day decisions.

第 4 步：起草原则（15 分钟）。分成小组，或保持整个团队（取决于团队大小），把排名靠前的原则起草成表达清晰的版本。对每条原则，定义它意味着什么、为什么必不可少，并给出一个具体例子让它落地。目标是把泛泛的想法转化为能指导日常决策的可执行指引。

Step 5: Discussion and ranking (15 minutes). Discuss the top-voted principles as a team, allowing people to advocate for principles they believe are essential. Rank the principles based on importance and relevance to your specific organization’s needs and challenges. This prioritization is beneficial when principles come into conflict during decision making.

第 5 步：讨论与排序（15 分钟）。作为团队讨论得票最高的那些原则，允许人们为自己认为必不可少的原则发声辩护。根据重要性、以及与本组织具体需求和挑战的相关性给原则排序。当决策过程中原则之间发生冲突时，这种优先级排序会很有用。

Step 6: Review (5 minutes). Examine the finalized list of principles, ensuring they are clear and actionable, and that they genuinely reflect the team’s values. Create a document outlining your principles and share it widely. Consider integrating them into your architecture decision records, code review checklists, and onboarding materials to ensure they’re referenced and utilized.

第 6 步：评审（5 分钟）。检查最终的原则清单，确保它们清晰、可执行，并真正反映团队的价值观。创建一份文档写明这些原则并广泛分享。考虑把它们纳入你的架构决策记录（ADR）、代码评审清单和新人上手材料，确保它们被引用、被使用。

This workshop approach transforms the abstract concept of technical principles into a concrete set of guidelines with broad team buy-in. The collaborative nature ensures that diverse perspectives are incorporated and that the final principles reflect the collective wisdom of your engineering team.

这种工作坊方式把“技术原则”这个抽象概念，转化为一套被团队广泛认同的具体指引。协作的本质保证了多元视角被纳入，最终的原则也能反映工程团队的集体智慧。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

In the StudioOps team, April ran the technical principles workshop with a twist. She started by having the team list their current pain points: Marcus complained about debugging Sarah’s frontend code without documentation, Sarah couldn’t understand Derek’s database-stored procedures, and Derek was frustrated by Marcus’s authentication system that required manual restarts. From these complaints, they established principles: “documentation before deployment” (no pull request merges without README updates), “boring technology first” (addressing their React version chaos), and “observable by default” (as they currently have no monitoring on half of their services). The senior engineers initially resisted the principles until April showed them that they had spent hours that quarter just figuring out each other’s code patterns. That’s potentially months of an engineer’s time lost to inconsistency.

在 StudioOps 团队，April 把技术原则工作坊做出了一点变体。她先让团队列出当下的痛点：Marcus 抱怨在没有文档的情况下调试 Sarah 的前端代码，Sarah 看不懂 Derek 的数据库存储过程，Derek 则被 Marcus 那套需要手动重启的认证系统搞得很烦。从这些抱怨出发，他们定下了几条原则：“部署前先写文档”（不更新 README 的 PR 不得合入）、“先用无聊技术”（解决他们 React 版本混乱的问题）、“默认可观测”（因为他们一半的服务目前连监控都没有）。资深工程师起初对这些原则很抵触，直到 April 给他们算了一笔账：仅仅这个季度，大家就在“琢磨彼此的代码套路”上花了好几个小时——这可能相当于一个工程师好几个月的时间，白白浪费在不一致上。

— 原书第 177 页 —

Living Your Principles

让原则活起来

To ensure these principles are lived, they also need active endorsement from leadership and champions across the team. This is often where those pesky staff and principal engineers earn their money, championing technical principles. However, it’s essential that all engineering leaders—from chief technology officers to engineering managers, as well as staff and principal engineers—must champion these technical principles. They ensure they become embedded in the organizational culture and influence every decision, from high-level strategic planning down to the nitty-gritty details of code development. This top-down endorsement helps ensure that the principles aren’t just dusty documents but are consistently followed.

要让这些原则真正被践行，还需要领导层和团队中各“倡导者”的积极背书。这些讨厌的 staff / principal 工程师们，往往就是在“为技术原则站台”这件事上挣到工资的。然而，所有工程领导者都必须为这些技术原则站台——从 CTO 到工程经理，再加上 staff / principal 工程师。他们要确保原则嵌入组织文化，影响从高层战略规划到代码开发琐碎细节的每一个决策。这种自上而下的背书能保证：原则不只是落灰的文档，而是被持续遵守。

Scaling Without Overengineering

在不过度设计的前提下扩展

After you have your foundation and principles, the most significant objective for your technical strategy is to let you scale without overengineering. Scaling without going overboard on engineering starts with a straightforward principle: keep it simple!

打好地基、立好原则之后，技术战略最重要的目标，就是让你能在不过度设计（overengineering）的前提下扩展。而“扩展但不过度”始于一个直截了当的原则：保持简单！

When designing your strategy and architecture, start with something simple. The whole approach comes down to the idea that simplicity is much more sophisticated than complexity. By avoiding unnecessary complications, you reduce the risk of introducing headaches and problems later on. You need to think about future scalability, but your strategy should mainly tackle today’s requirements. Over-optimizing for some hypothetical future that might never happen can waste resources and make things way more complex than they need to be. Instead, let your scaling decisions be guided by real-world demand and data, ensuring that any changes respond to real needs rather than hypothetical scenarios.

设计战略和架构时，从简单的东西起步。整个思路归结为一句话：简洁比复杂要高级得多。避免不必要的复杂化，你就降低了日后自找麻烦、自添问题的风险。你确实需要考虑未来的可扩展性，但战略主要应当解决当下的需求。为某个也许永远不会发生的假想未来过度优化，只会浪费资源，让事情比必要的复杂得多。相反，让扩展决策由真实需求和数据来牵引，确保任何变更都是对真实需求的回应，而不是对假想场景的回应。

This isn’t to say you shouldn’t think about future needs, but it’s important to strike the right balance. Investing in good technology means planning for what you need now and where you might expand later. You likely don’t need to build the most advanced or complex world right off the bat; what’s essential is having a clear plan that lets your system evolve gracefully over time. This approach helps ensure that your system can scale efficiently as your business grows and that you can make incremental improvements without breaking everything.

这并不是说你不该考虑未来需求，而是要把握好平衡。在好技术上投入，意味着既要规划现在需要什么，也要规划以后可能往哪里扩展。你大概率不需要一上来就造一个最先进、最复杂的世界；关键是要有一份清晰的计划，让你的系统能随时间优雅演进。这种方式能保证：业务增长时系统能高效扩展，你也能在不把一切搞崩的前提下做增量改进。

The key trade-off decisions in scaling come down to differentiation versus commodity and just-in-time scalability. Choose to build only what differentiates your business; buy everything else. Scale only when you have evidence that you need to, not based on optimistic projections.

扩展中最关键的权衡决策，归结为两点：差异化 vs 商品化，以及准时制（just-in-time）扩展。只造那些能让你的业务与众不同的东西，其余一切都买。只有当你有证据表明确实需要扩展时才扩展，而不是基于乐观的预测。

An excellent example is database design and selection. If you’re building most applications, choosing PostgreSQL as your first database is a strong choice. It’s performant, scales well, is well represented and supported by cloud providers, and has a healthy ecosystem for ORMs (object–relational mapping), tooling, and support for numerous languages and frameworks.

一个绝佳的例子是数据库设计与选型。如果你在构建大多数应用，把 PostgreSQL 作为第一个数据库是很强的选择。它性能好、扩展性好、云厂商广泛支持，在 ORM（对象关系映射）、工具链以及对众多语言和框架的支持方面都有健康的生态。

— 原书第 178 页 —

There is extensive documentation and many examples online that provide guidance on how to work with, tune, and configure it for various scenarios. It’s almost “you won’t get fired for buying IBM” good. Combine this with a well-designed schema—for example, typing integer fields that might grow as large as bigint instead of integer—and you can achieve a solid solution without unnecessary complexity, investment, or overhead. You’re probably pretty well set up if your product takes off.

网上有大量文档和示例，指导你如何在各种场景下使用、调优和配置它。它几乎好到那种“买 IBM 不会被炒鱿鱼”的程度。再配合一个设计良好的 schema——例如把可能长大的整数字段直接定义成 bigint 而不是 integer——你就能在不引入不必要复杂度、投入或开销的情况下，得到一个扎实的解决方案。如果你的产品真的火了，这套底子大概率也撑得住。

On the other hand, different choices make sense for different contexts. SQLite excels for embedded applications or development environments. In addition, CockroachDB becomes valuable when you genuinely need global distribution and can afford the operational complexity. The key is matching the technology to your actual requirements, not your imagined future state.

另一方面，不同语境下有不同的合理选择。SQLite 在嵌入式应用或开发环境中表现出色；而当你真的需要全球分布式、并且负担得起其运维复杂度时，CockroachDB 就变得有价值。关键是让技术匹配你的真实需求，而不是你想象中的未来状态。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April discovered that the StudioOps team was running MongoDB for user data, PostgreSQL for application data, Redis for caching, Elasticsearch for logs, and DynamoDB for session data. When she asked why, the answer was always “That’s what [specific senior engineer] knows best.” The monthly Amazon Web Services (AWS) bill was $45,000, with $12,000 just for running five different database systems. April’s strategy was to consolidate to PostgreSQL for everything except caching (keeping Redis). PostgreSQL can handle JSON documents (replacing MongoDB), has full-text search (replacing basic Elasticsearch use cases) and, with proper indexing, can easily handle session storage (replacing DynamoDB). This isn’t about PostgreSQL being perfect; it’s about reducing operational complexity. The team can now gain a deep understanding of one database, rather than trying to understand five. The AWS bill dropped to $31,000, and deployment time improved by 40% as they weren’t coordinating across five different datastores.

April 发现 StudioOps 团队的架构是：用户数据用 MongoDB、应用数据用 PostgreSQL、缓存用 Redis、日志用 Elasticsearch、会话数据用 DynamoDB。她问为什么，答案永远是“那位[某位资深工程师]最懂这个”。每月的 AWS 账单是 45,000 美元，其中光跑五套不同数据库就占了 12,000 美元。April 的策略是：除了缓存（保留 Redis）之外，全部收敛到 PostgreSQL。PostgreSQL 能处理 JSON 文档（替代 MongoDB）、有全文检索（替代 Elasticsearch 的基础用法），配合合适的索引也能轻松承担会话存储（替代 DynamoDB）。这不是说 PostgreSQL 完美无缺，而是为了降低运维复杂度。团队现在可以深入吃透一个数据库，而不是费力去理解五个。AWS 账单降到了 31,000 美元，部署时间缩短了 40%——因为他们不再需要在五个数据存储之间协调了。

In addition to keeping things simple, leveraging SaaS, off-the-shelf, and cloud-based solutions is a game changer for building scalable systems without overengineering. Modern cloud platforms like AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure provide elastic and flexible infrastructure options that let you roll with unexpected demand spikes. These services enable you to scale resources up or down as needed, so you don’t have to build some crazy complex architecture that tries to predict every possible future scenario. This approach saves resources and makes your system more adaptable to real-time usage patterns.

除了保持简单，善用 SaaS、现成产品和云原生解决方案，对于“在不过度设计的前提下构建可扩展系统”是一个颠覆性的杠杆。AWS、Google Cloud、Microsoft Azure 这类现代云平台提供弹性、灵活的基础设施选项，让你能应对意料之外的流量峰值。这些服务让你按需伸缩资源，于是你不必去造一套试图预测每一种未来场景的疯狂复杂架构。这种方式既省资源，又让系统更能适应实时使用模式。

Footnote: The bigint type has a larger range than the int type (–2147483648 to +2147483647 compared with –9223372036854775808 to +9223372036854775807).

脚注：bigint 类型的取值范围比 int 更大（int 为 −2147483648 到 +2147483647，bigint 为 −9223372036854775808 到 +9223372036854775807）。

— 原书第 179 页 —

Making the right build-versus-buy decisions is also key to a good strategy. Through‐out the book, we’ve discussed buying products and services that are not your core business. If you’re not in the business of building a database, don’t build a database. This seems self-evident in cloud services like computing and storage, as well as adjacent services like workflows, ticketing, knowledge management, and email, but don’t stop there. Juan works in a large corporation with a strong focus on customer service. That organization developed tools to automate customer management tasks, including ticketing and service management. These functions are bread and butter for most service organizations and don’t represent business differentiation. A new strategy—buying the right tools instead of building them, and focusing on the quality and performance of service delivery—was introduced to correct that.

做出正确的“自建 vs 采购”（build vs buy）决策，也是好战略的关键。本书反复讲过：非核心业务的产品和服务，能买就买。如果你的业务不是造数据库，就别自己造数据库。这一点在计算、存储这类云服务，以及工作流、工单、知识管理、邮件这类相邻服务上似乎不言自明，但不要停在这里。Juan 曾在一家高度重视客户服务的大公司工作。那家组织自己开发了工具来自动化客户管理任务，包括工单和服务管理。对大多数服务型组织来说，这些功能是家常便饭，并不构成业务差异化。后来他们引入了一项新战略——买合适的工具而不是自建，把精力聚焦在服务交付的质量与性能上——来纠正这一点。

The term “adaptable architecture” means systems designed to accommodate change without requiring complete rewrites. This includes using microservices where appro priate (but not by default), implementing proper abstraction layers, maintaining clear API boundaries, and choosing technologies with strong ecosystems that can grow with you. The goal is to build systems that can evolve incrementally rather than requiring periodic massive overhauls.

“可适应架构”（adaptable architecture）这个词，指的是那些能容纳变化、而不必整体重写的系统。这包括：在合适的场景下使用微服务（但不是默认就用）、实现恰当的抽象层、维护清晰的 API 边界，以及选择生态强大、能陪你一起成长的技术。目标是构建可以增量演进的系统，而不是每隔一段时间就要大动干戈地重做一遍。

Choose Boring Technology

选择无聊技术

Every technical decision involves trade-offs. If you want more scale, that might cost more. If you want better performance, you might have to sacrifice some flexibility. If you want to use the latest tech, then you’ll have a smaller hiring pool of engineers who know it. Be explicit about what you’re prioritizing—and why—throughout your strategy development and implementation.

每一个技术决策都包含权衡。想要更大的规模，可能要花更多钱；想要更好的性能，可能要牺牲一些灵活性；想用最新的技术，那么懂它的工程师招聘池就更小。在制定和落地战略的全过程中，都要明确你在优先什么、以及为什么。

A particularly important lesson for engineers, especially those making technology choices for the first time, is to resist the temptation of chasing shiny new tech just because it’s trendy. There’s a common pitfall where a team feels they need to rewrite their entire codebase in the hottest new programming language or adopt the framework everyone is talking about on Hacker News without considering the long-term benefits. The engineer Dan McKinley has a maxim: choose boring technol‐ogy. He posits that you have a certain number of “innovation tokens.” You spend an innovation token each time you make a technology choice that isn’t “boring”:

对工程师——尤其是第一次做技术选型的工程师——来说，一条特别重要的教训是：抵挡住“因为时髦就追逐新奇技术”的诱惑。一个常见的坑是：团队觉得必须用最火的新语言重写整个代码库，或者采用 Hacker News 上人人都在聊的那个框架，却不去想长期收益。工程师 Dan McKinley 有一句格言：选择无聊技术。他提出：你拥有一定数量的“创新代币”（innovation tokens）；每当你做了一个不那么“无聊”的技术选择，就花掉一枚：

Let’s say every company gets about three innovation tokens. You can spend these however you want, but the supply is fixed for a long while. You might get a few more after you achieve a certain level of stability and maturity, but the general tendency is to overestimate the contents of your wallet. Clearly this model is approximate, but I think it helps.

假设每家公司大约有三枚创新代币。你想怎么花都行，但供给在很长一段时间内是固定的。当你达到一定的稳定性和成熟度之后，可能会再得到几枚；但总体上，人们总是高估自己钱包里的余额。显然这个模型是近似的，但我觉得它有用。

If you choose to write your website in NodeJS, you just spent one of your innovation tokens. If you choose to use MongoDB, you just spent one of your innovation tokens. If you choose to use service discovery tech that’s existed for a year or less, you just spent one of your innovation tokens. If you choose to write your own database, oh god, you’re in trouble.

如果你选择用 NodeJS 写网站，你刚花掉了一枚创新代币。如果你选择用 MongoDB，刚花掉一枚。如果你选择用一种问世还不到一年的服务发现技术，又花掉一枚。如果你选择自己写数据库——天哪，你麻烦大了。

Any of those choices might be sensible if you’re a javascript consultancy, or a database company. But you’re probably not. You’re probably working for a company that is at least ostensibly rethinking global commerce or reinventing payments on the web or pursuing some other suitably epic mission. In that context, devoting any of your limited attention to innovating ssh is an excellent way to fail. Or at best, delay success.

如果你是一家 JavaScript 咨询公司，或者一家数据库公司，以上任何选择都可能是合理的。但你大概率不是。你大概率在一家表面上至少是在“重新定义全球商业”、或“重构网络支付”、或追求其他类似史诗使命的公司工作。在这种语境下，把有限的注意力投入到“创新 ssh”上，是一条绝佳的失败之路；往好里说，也只是推迟成功。

What counts as boring? That’s a little tricky. “Boring” should not be conflated with “bad.” There is technology out there that is both boring and bad. You should not use any of that. But there are many choices of technology that are boring and good, or at least good enough. MySQL is boring. Postgres is boring. PHP is boring. Python is boring. Memcached is boring. Squid is boring. Cron is boring.

什么算“无聊”？这有点微妙。“无聊”不应等同于“糟糕”。世上确实既有聊又糟糕的技术，那种你一样都不该用。但也有很多无聊且好用、或至少足够好用的技术。MySQL 很无聊，Postgres 很无聊，PHP 很无聊，Python 很无聊，Memcached 很无聊，Squid 很无聊，Cron 很无聊。

— 原书第 180 页 —

The definition of boring technology naturally evolves. These days, we’d probably not say Node.js was a risky choice (though your mileage may vary), but the underlying framework is still consistent. In modern times, we’d put choices like “We should use Kubernetes” or “Gee, we need a service mesh” into that innovation token bucket; again, your mileage may vary.

“无聊技术”的定义会自然演进。如今我们大概不会说 Node.js 是个冒险的选择（当然，具体情况因人而异），但底层框架仍然一致。放到今天，我们会把“我们该用 Kubernetes”或“哎呀，我们需要一个 service mesh”这类选择丢进创新代币的桶里；同样，具体情况因人而异。

You should resist the superficial appeal of jumping into tech that promises (poten‐tially tiny) gains in innovation but often results in significant overhead, instability, and technical debt. Constantly rewriting code to keep up with the latest trends can lead to a ton of unnecessary work, and it might undermine the stability of your product and deeply frustrate your team. You’ve got to carefully weigh the potential benefits against the costs, ensuring that any move to new technologies is justified by improved performance, easier maintenance, or better scalability.

你应当抵制这种技术的表面诱惑：它承诺在创新上带来（可能微乎其微的）收益，却往往带来巨大的开销、不稳定性和技术债。为了追赶最新潮流而不断重写代码，会导致大量不必要的工作，还可能损害产品稳定性、让团队深受挫败。你必须仔细权衡潜在收益与成本，确保任何向新技术的迁移都能用“性能提升、更易维护、或更好的可扩展性”来证明其正当性。

Every effort you invest into refactoring is also an effort that you are not investing in your product(s) and their development. We discussed the whys of prioritization in Chapter 6; this is a good time to ensure that you factor those into any architectural decisions you make.

你投入到重构上的每一分精力，同时也是没有投入到产品及其开发上的精力。我们在第 6 章讨论过优先级排序的“为什么”；现在正是把那些考量代入你所做任何架构决策的好时机。

Ultimately, your programming language or framework choice should be driven by your business needs rather than what looks cool in a blog post. The most modern or hyped technology isn’t always the best fit for every organization, especially consid‐ering its impact on team dynamics, hiring, and long-term maintainability. A smart strategy is to optimize and refine what you have already when it makes sense, rather than embarking on a complete rewrite that might not yield enough advantages to justify all the blood, sweat, and tears. Keeping business objectives front and center ensures that your technology choices align with your strategic goals and provide a stable foundation for sustainable growth.

归根结底，编程语言或框架的选择应当由业务需求驱动，而不是由某篇博客里看起来很酷的东西驱动。最现代、最被热捧的技术，并不总是最适合每个组织的——尤其要考虑它对团队协作、招聘和长期可维护性的影响。聪明的战略是：在合理的情况下，优化和打磨你已有的东西，而不是启动一场彻底重写——那种重写带来的好处可能根本抵不上你付出的血汗。把业务目标放在最中心，能确保技术选择与战略目标对齐，为可持续增长提供稳定地基。

— 原书第 181 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April faced this directly when Marcus proposed rewriting the authentication system in Rust “for better performance.” April did the math: their auth service handles 1,000 requests per second at peak, with p99 latency of 50 ms using boring old Node.js. Moving to Rust might drop that to 20 ms, but at what cost? They’d need to hire Rust developers (currently zero on the team), maintain a separate deployment pipeline, and train the juniors on yet another language. April framed it in innovation tokens: “We’re already spending one token on our custom animation rendering engine—that’s our competitive advantage—and another on the real-time collaboration features that differentiate us. Do we really want to spend our last token on making authentication 30 ms faster when customers have never complained about auth speed?” The proposal was withdrawn, and they instead spent a week optimizing the Node.js implementation, achieving 35 ms p99 with technology the whole team understands.

April 直接遇上了这种事：Marcus 提议用 Rust 重写认证系统，“以获得更好的性能”。April 算了一笔账：他们的认证服务峰值每秒处理 1,000 个请求，用老旧的 Node.js 时 p99 延迟是 50 毫秒。换成 Rust 也许能降到 20 毫秒，但代价是什么？他们得招 Rust 开发（团队里目前一个都没有）、维护一套独立的部署流水线，还要用又一门语言培训初级工程师。April 用创新代币的框架来提问：“我们已经在自研发动画渲染引擎上花了一枚代币——那是我们的竞争优势——又在实时协作功能上花了一枚，那是我们的差异化。客户从来没抱怨过认证速度，我们真的要把最后一枚代币花在让认证快 30 毫秒上吗？”提案被撤回，他们转而花了一周优化 Node.js 实现，用全队都懂的技术把 p99 做到了 35 毫秒。

Adopting new technologies should create specific, measurable value: reducing operational costs, increasing development velocity, expanding addressable markets, improving customer satisfaction metrics, or enabling new revenue streams. If you can’t articulate how a technology choice drives one of these outcomes, you’re proba‐bly spending innovation tokens unwisely.

采用新技术应当创造具体、可度量的价值：降低运维成本、提升开发速度、扩大可触达市场、改善客户满意度指标，或带来新的收入流。如果你说不清一项技术选择如何驱动了上述结果之一，那你很可能在不明智地花掉创新代币。

Scaling without overengineering involves striking a balance, valuing simplicity, lever‐aging scalable cloud services, and (carefully and cautiously) investing in adaptable architecture. It requires a disciplined look at whether adopting new technologies (spending those innovation tokens) adds value or introduces unnecessary complexity. Keeping business needs in focus ensures that the tools and frameworks you choose enhance operational efficiency and long-term stability rather than being pursued because they’re the latest fad.

“不过度设计地扩展”需要把握平衡：重视简洁、善用可扩展的云服务，并（谨慎地、小心翼翼地）投资于可适应架构。它要求你纪律严明地审视：采用新技术（花掉那些创新代币）到底是在增加价值，还是在引入不必要的复杂度。把业务需求放在焦点上，能确保你选择的工具和框架提升运维效率与长期稳定性，而不是因为它们是最新潮流才被追逐。

Developing Your Technical Strategy

制定你的技术战略

We’ve got the pieces of our strategy now: insights into our current world, a model for building without overengineering, and a set of technical principles. From these, creating a technical strategy is like planning a holiday; you need to know your destination, understand how you get there, and prepare for unexpected detours.

现在我们已经有了战略的几块拼图：对当下世界的洞察、一套“不过度设计地构建”的模型，以及一组技术原则。基于这些去创造技术战略，就像规划一次假期：你要知道目的地、搞清楚怎么去，并为意料之外的绕道做好准备。

At its core, a solid technical strategy connects your technology decisions to your company’s big-picture goals, ensuring that everything you build supports the broader vision. When done well, it aligns your product vision (what you want to build) with your technical approach (how you’ll build it), keeping your team focused and your products on target.

从根本上说，一套扎实的技术战略把你的技术决策与公司的大目标连接起来，确保你所构建的一切都服务于更宏大的愿景。做得好时，它会把产品愿景（你想造什么）与技术路径（你要怎么造）对齐，让团队保持专注、产品不偏靶。

— 原书第 182 页 —

We like a well-planned trip. Indeed, James’ travel planning spreadsheets are famous among our friends, primarily for their multilayered contingency management. We know, however, that you can’t plan for every contingency in chaotic environments. So, in a chaotic environment, a strong technical strategy isn’t static; it’s dynamic, fluid, and adapts to changing conditions. This manifests most clearly in your choice of planning time frames, windows, and granularity.

我们喜欢计划周密的旅行。说真的，James 的旅行规划表在朋友圈里是出了名的，主要因为它有层层叠叠的应急预案。但我们也知道，在混乱环境里，你没法为每种意外都做好计划。因此，在混乱环境中，一套强有力的技术战略不是静态的，而是动态的、流动的，能随条件变化而调整。这一点最鲜明地体现在你对规划时间跨度、时间窗口和颗粒度的选择上。

Choosing Granularity

选择颗粒度

We recommend a practical time window. For many chaotic organizations, a quarter is a lifetime, and for others, planning for an entire year is feasible (while we question that, it’s possible). You need enough time to invest in developing a meaningful and aspirational strategy, but not so much that the objectives become less aspirational than delusional. If you do want to look at the future, then dial down the level of granularity—for example, with detailed granularity in Q1, medium granularity in Q2 and Q3, and low granularity in Q4. Review the plan monthly to ensure you’re on track and that the strategy aligns with reality.

我们建议一个务实的时间窗口。对许多混乱组织来说，一个季度就是一辈子；而对另一些组织，规划一整年是可行的（虽然我们对此存疑，但它确实可能）。你需要足够的时间去投入，打磨出一套有意义、有愿景的战略；但时间又不能长到让目标从“有愿景”变成“妄想”。如果你确实想看得远一些，那就调低颗粒度——例如 Q1 详细规划、Q2 和 Q3 中等颗粒度、Q4 粗线条。每月复盘计划，确保你在正轨上、战略与现实保持对齐。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April’s StudioOps quarterly planning demonstrates practical granularity:

April 在 StudioOps 的季度规划展示了务实的颗粒度：

Q1 (high detail). Consolidate to PostgreSQL (weeks 1–4), implement monitoring on all services (weeks 5–8), and standardize API patterns to REST (weeks 9–12).

Q1（高细节）。收敛到 PostgreSQL（第 1–4 周）、为所有服务落地监控（第 5–8 周）、把 API 模式标准化为 REST（第 9–12 周）。

Q2 (medium detail). Complete authentication system consolidation, begin frontend standardization to React 18, and improve the CI/CD pipeline.

Q2（中等细节）。完成认证系统收敛、开始把前端标准化到 React 18、改进 CI/CD 流水线。

Q3 (low detail). Scale infrastructure for expected customer growth, and address remaining technical debt.

Q3（低细节）。为预期的客户增长扩展基础设施，并处理剩余技术债。

Q4 (directional only). Establish platform stability and optimization focus.

Q4（只定方向）。确立平台稳定性与优化的重点方向。

She reviewed this monthly, and by week 6 realized the PostgreSQL consolidation was taking longer than expected. Rather than rushing, she adjusted Q1 to focus on just MongoDB-to-PostgreSQL migration, pushing the DynamoDB work to Q2. In this exam‐ple, you can see how the strategy remains intact, but the tactics adapt to reality.

她每月复盘一次，到第 6 周时意识到 PostgreSQL 收敛比预期更耗时。她没有赶工，而是把 Q1 调整为只专注于 MongoDB 到 PostgreSQL 的迁移，把 DynamoDB 的工作推到 Q2。在这个例子里，你能看到战略保持不变，但战术随现实而调整。

— 原书第 183 页 —

Balancing Flexibility with Direction

在灵活性与方向感之间平衡

Remember our discussion about scaling without overengineering? The same princi‐ple applies to your technical strategy. You want just enough structure to provide clear direction without becoming so rigid that you can’t adapt when surprises pop up (and they always do).

还记得我们关于“不过度设计地扩展”的讨论吗？同样的原则也适用于你的技术战略。你需要刚刚好的结构：既能提供清晰方向，又不至于僵硬到意外冒出来时无法适应（而意外总是会冒出来）。

Think of your strategy as a compass rather than a GPS with turn-by-turn directions. It points you in the right direction while leaving room to navigate around obstacles as they appear. This is especially important when we reflect on our technical principles; they serve as guardrails that help you stay on track, not concrete barriers that lock you into a single path.

把战略想象成指南针，而不是一套逐向导航的 GPS。它给你指出正确方向，同时留出空间，让你在障碍物出现时绕行。当我们回头看技术原则时这一点尤其重要：它们是帮你保持在轨道上的护栏，而不是把你锁死在单一路径上的混凝土高墙。

Collaborative Development

协作式制定

Remember that the best strategies aren’t crafted in isolation. As we recommended a collaborative approach to developing technical principles, your strategy should be designed with input from your team. The engineers who will implement the strategy, the product folks who will build on top of it, and the leadership who will support it should all have a voice.

记住：最好的战略不是闭门造车造出来的。正如我们建议用协作方式打磨技术原则，你的战略也应当在团队输入下设计。将落地这一战略的工程师、在其上构建产品的产品同事、以及将为它提供支持的领导层，都应当有发言权。

This doesn’t mean making decisions by committee (because that’s a recipe for the most watered-down, least useful strategy possible). But it does mean getting diverse perspectives and buy-in before you finalize your approach. The people implementing the strategy need to understand and believe in it; otherwise, it will just gather digital dust in your shared drive. We explore this more in Chapter 9, where we go into depth into collaborative decision making.

这并不意味着由委员会来做决策（因为那几乎必然产出最稀释、最没用的战略）。但它确实意味着：在定稿之前，你要拿到多元视角和认同。执行战略的人必须理解它、相信它；否则它只会在你的共享盘里积数字灰尘。我们会在第 9 章更深入地探讨这一点，那里会深入讲解协作式决策。

Elements of a Technical Strategy Document

技术战略文档的要素

In this subsection, we’ll walk through what a solid technical strategy and architecture document should include, with brief explanations of each section.

本小节我们过一遍一份扎实的技术战略与架构文档应当包含什么，并简要解释每一节。

Introduction and overview. Clearly state the document’s purpose, audience, and intended outcomes. Provide context so your audience, both within your team and external to it, can immediately grasp its significance and relevance.

引言与概览。清楚说明文档的目的、受众和预期成果。提供背景，让你的受众——无论是团队内部还是外部——都能立刻理解它的重要性与相关性。

Strategic vision and objectives. Articulate how technology directly supports the organization’s broader mission and strategic priorities. Linking technology decisions to strategic goals clarifies the rationale behind every technical initiative. Suppose your organization has goals, such as quarterly sales goals. In that case, this is where you indicate how your work contributes to that objective or falls under product initiatives that support those goals. For example, we can’t release version 2 of the product unless we can support more users.

战略愿景与目标。阐明技术如何直接支撑组织更宏大的使命与战略优先级。把技术决策与战略目标挂钩，能让每项技术举措背后的理由都清晰可见。假设你的组织有目标，比如季度销售目标；那么这里就要说明你的工作如何贡献于该目标，或归属于支撑这些目标的产品举措。例如：除非我们能支持更多用户，否则就无法发布产品的 v2。

— 原书第 184 页 —

If you don’t have strategic goals in the larger organization, then you might tie your goals directly to your product roadmap.

如果在更大的组织层面没有战略目标，那么你可以把自己的目标直接挂到产品路线图上。

Current technology landscape. Document existing technologies, tools, and systems, including their current strengths and weaknesses. This is where the foundational insights you gain are placed, and as you improve the environment, this section is refreshed with the current reality.

当前技术格局。记录现有的技术、工具和系统，包括它们当前的优势与劣势。这一节就是安放你所获得的基础洞察的地方；随着你改进环境，这一节也要按当前现实刷新。

Future state landscape. This is the core of your strategy; the list of things you will do. Here, we describe your vision for the future state landscape: what tools and technologies will be deprecated, what will evolve, and what will be decommissioned. We also like to include future state operations and processes—for example, if you don’t have an incident management and incident review process, this is where you’d specify that you intend to have one. Like the previous section, this section evolves as your strategy is implemented.

未来状态格局。这是你战略的核心：你将要做的事情的清单。这里描述你对未来格局的愿景：哪些工具和技术会被弃用、哪些会演进、哪些会被下线。我们还喜欢把未来的运维与流程也纳入其中——例如，如果你目前没有事件管理与事件复盘流程，这里就要写明你打算建立一套。和上一节一样，本节也会随战略的落地而演进。

Technical principles. This is where your technical principles live or are cited. Refer back to the principles we discussed earlier, the ones that guide your engineering decisions and help you avoid making things worse, even in chaotic environments.

技术原则。技术原则在这里安家，或被引用。回指我们前面讨论过的那些原则——那些指导你工程决策、帮你即便在混乱环境中也不把事情搞得更糟的原则。

Implementation roadmap. Provide a phased plan outlining how to transition from your current to your desired state. Chapter 6 discussed prioritization and planning extensively; many of the techniques articulated there can help you structure the plan. This roadmap exists in relation to your product roadmap. Some organizations run parallel tracks with allocated “lanes” for technical work versus product features (e.g., 70% product development, 30% technical development). Others opportunistically pull technical items into sprints when they align with product work. The key is being explicit about how technical and product work interweave, whether that’s through dedicated technical sprints, percentage allocations, or by embedding technical work within feature development.

实施路线图。给出一份分阶段计划，概述如何从当前状态过渡到期望状态。第 6 章大量讨论了优先级与规划，那里讲的许多技巧可以帮你组织这份计划。这条路线图是相对于你的产品路线图而存在的。有些组织并行运行多条轨道，为技术工作和产品功能分配不同“车道”（例如 70% 产品开发、30% 技术开发）；另一些组织则在技术项与产品工作对齐时，见机把它们拉进 sprint。关键是要讲清楚：技术工作与产品工作是如何交织的——无论是通过专门的技术 sprint、百分比分配，还是把技术工作嵌入功能开发之中。

People, resources, and teams. Clearly describe how people and resources will be allocated, including team members, tools, and budgets. One aspect of your technical strategy may be team changes, such as growing a team, reorganizing a team, or redefining or redeploying people to better meet your needs.

人员、资源与团队。清楚说明人员和资源将如何分配，包括团队成员、工具和预算。你的技术战略的一个方面可能是团队变化，比如扩编团队、重组团队，或重新定义、重新部署人员以更好地满足需求。

— 原书第 185 页 —

Risk management and contingency planning. Identify and assess potential risks, including technical, financial, and operational factors. This is the “what could go wrong” section. You can’t plan for every risk or plan contingencies for every potential risk, but you can likely identify high-level risks. For example, you might identify a risk like the following:

风险管理与应急预案。识别并评估潜在风险，包括技术、财务和运营因素。这是“可能出什么岔子”的那一节。你没法为每一个风险做计划、或为每一个潜在风险都准备应急预案，但你大概能识别出高层风险。例如，你可以识别出这样一个风险：

Risk. Our application relies on a third-party authentication service that has experienced three outages in the past six months, which has directly impacted our users’ experience of the platform.

风险。我们的应用依赖一个第三方认证服务，该服务在过去六个月里已经出过三次故障，直接影响了用户对平台的使用体验。

Mitigant. By Q2, implement a fallback authentication method that can be activated within five minutes of detecting an outage in the primary service. Additionally, establish a monitoring system that alerts the on-call engineer when the service’s response time exceeds two seconds. Over the longer term, consider a replacement for the platform.

缓解措施。到 Q2，实现一种备用认证方式，能在检测到主服务故障的五分钟内激活。此外，建立一套监控，当服务响应时间超过两秒时告警值班工程师。更长期来看，考虑替换该平台。

Here is another example:

再举一个例子：

Risk. We have a severe knowledge silo where only one engineer (Rajiv) understands our payment processing system, creating a significant bus factor problem.

风险。我们存在严重的知识孤岛：只有一位工程师（Rajiv）理解支付处理系统，造成了显著的巴士因子（bus factor）问题。

Mitigant. Schedule a weekly knowledge-sharing session where Rajiv walks another engineer through one payment system component. Document all sessions and store them in our knowledge base. By the end of Q3, ensure at least two additional engineers can confidently support the payment system.

缓解措施。每周安排一次知识分享会，由 Rajiv 带另一位工程师过一遍支付系统的一个组件。把每次会议都文档化并存入知识库。到 Q3 结束时，确保至少再有两位工程师能有底气地支持支付系统。

Consider this technical debt example:

再看一个技术债的例子：

Risk. Our monolithic codebase is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain, with bug fixes taking 30% longer than they did six months ago.

风险。我们的单体代码库越来越难维护，bug 修复比六个月前多花 30% 的时间。

Mitigant. Begin incremental migration to a microservices architecture, starting with the most frequently changed components. Set a goal to extract two services by the end of Q2, with clear interfaces between them and the remaining monolith.

缓解措施。开始向微服务架构做增量迁移，从最频繁变更的组件开始。设一个目标：到 Q2 结束时拆出两个服务，并在它们与剩余单体之间定义清晰接口。

Concrete examples make risk management actionable. Consider risks around scaling (e.g., if traffic increases 10 times), team changes (e.g., if your key architect leaves), vendor dependencies (e.g., if AWS has an extended outage), and technical evolution (e.g., if your framework becomes unsupported). The key is to be specific about both

具体的例子让风险管理可落地。考虑围绕扩展（例如流量增长 10 倍）、团队变动（例如你的关键架构师离职）、厂商依赖（例如 AWS 长时间宕机）和技术演进（例如你用的框架不再被维护）的风险。关键是要把两件事都讲具体：

— 原书第 186 页 —

the risk (ideally with some quantification of its impact) and the concrete actions you will take to address it, including time frames and success criteria.

风险（最好对其影响有一些量化），以及你为应对它将采取的具体行动，包括时间框架和成功标准。

Governance and decision-making processes. Define decision-making processes and structures, specifying roles, responsibilities, and review procedures. Effective governance ensures alignment, consistency, and accountability throughout the project lifecycle. In Chapter 9, we’ll discuss implementation governance when we introduce requests for comments (or RFCs).

治理与决策流程。定义决策流程与结构，明确角色、职责和评审程序。有效的治理能在整个项目生命周期内保证对齐、一致性和问责。在第 9 章，我们会在引入征求意见稿（RFC）时讨论实施治理。

Monitoring, metrics, and continuous improvement. Outline methods for tracking progress and measuring success. We discuss metrics more in Chapter 10, but every strategy needs qualitative and quantitative metrics to measure progress and success—or failure. It’s also important to establish checkpoints, such as every two sprints or once a month, where you pause, digest your current state and the metrics, and determine what might need to be adjusted, improved, or terminated.

监控、指标与持续改进。概述追踪进展和度量成功的方法。我们会在第 10 章更详细地讨论指标，但每一套战略都需要定性与定量指标来衡量进展与成功——或失败。同样重要的是建立检查点，例如每两个 sprint 或每月一次：你停下来，消化当前状态与指标，判断哪些东西可能需要调整、改进或终止。

The Living Document Approach

活文档方式

The most critical thing to understand about your technical strategy document is that it’s not meant to be static. Much like the system architecture diagram James created on his first day at the startup, which we discussed at the beginning of this chapter, your strategy document should evolve as your understanding deepens and conditions change.

关于技术战略文档，最关键的一点是：它不是静态的。就像我们在本章开头讨论过的 James 入职第一天画的那张系统架构图一样，你的战略文档应当随着你理解的加深和条件的变化而演进。

We recommend treating it as a living document. We discussed scheduling regular reviews, either monthly or quarterly, which is a good cadence for most organizations. These reviews enable you to revisit the strategy, assess progress, and make updates based on what you’ve learned. This keeps it relevant and avoids the all-too-common fate of strategy documents: forgotten in some digital folder, never to be opened again.

我们建议把它当作活文档来对待。我们讨论过安排定期复盘——每月或每季度，对大多数组织这是不错的节奏。这些复盘让你能重访战略、评估进展，并根据学到的东西做更新。这能让它始终保持相关性，避免战略文档最常见的命运：被遗忘在某个数字文件夹里，再也没人打开。

However, creating a technical strategy document is just the beginning. Even the best-crafted strategy is worthless if it doesn’t translate into actual change in how your team works and what you build. Let’s discuss bringing your strategy to life in your organization’s messy day-to-day reality.

然而，写出一份技术战略文档只是开始。如果它不能转化为团队工作方式和所构建之物的真实改变，再好的战略也一文不值。下面我们讨论如何在组织乱糟糟的日常现实中，让战略真正活起来。

Making Technical Strategies Real

让技术战略落地

So, you’ve got a slick strategy document—congrats! But as anyone who’s ever created a PowerPoint deck knows, pretty slides don’t magically translate into real-world change. Let’s discuss how to make this happen in your organization’s messy reality.

好，你现在有了一份漂亮的战略文档——恭喜！但任何做过 PPT 的人都知道：漂亮的幻灯片不会魔法般地转化为现实世界的改变。下面我们讨论如何在组织乱糟糟的现实中把它变成现实。

Most strategies fail when they move from “Here’s what we should do” to “We’re actually doing it.” You have to juggle multiple challenges at once—and it can feel like trying to solve a Rubik’s Cube while riding a unicycle. We’ve identified some guiding principles for implementation that should help you keep on track, all of which tie back to the technical principles you’ve established.

大多数战略，都是在从“我们应该做什么”走向“我们真的在做了”的那一步上失败的。你必须同时玩转多个挑战——那种感觉就像骑独轮车还试图解魔方。我们总结了一些实施上的指导原则，应该能帮你保持正轨；它们全部都回扣到你已经确立的技术原则。

— 原书第 187 页 —

Resource allocation (without burning everyone out). Your most precious resource is your people. Be thoughtful about matching tasks with team members. Nobody wants to be the person assigned to “fix the legacy monolith” for the fourth quarter in a row. Spread the love (and the difficulties) around. Ensure people have the necessary tools and time, and don’t expect them to work nights and weekends to meet arbitrary deadlines. That may work short-term, but you’ll be writing new job ads before you know it. Your poor planning should not constitute an emergency for your team.

资源分配（但不要把所有人都榨干）。你最宝贵的资源是人。把任务和团队成员匹配时要用心。没人愿意连续第四个季度被派去“修那个遗留单体”。把爱（和困难）分摊开。确保大家有必要的工具和时间，不要指望他们靠熬夜和周末去赶武断的死线。短期也许行得通，但不知不觉你就得写新的招聘广告了。你糟糕的计划，不应构成团队的紧急情况。

Picking tech that won’t make future-you curse past-you. Choosing tech is like getting a tattoo: it’ll be with you for a long time, or it’ll cost you dearly to remove it, so choose wisely. We have already discussed “choosing boring technology” and not chasing shiny objects, but it’s worth repeating. Ask yourself, “Will this solve our actual problems?” and “Can we maintain this when the person who championed it inevitably leaves?” Remember, you’re not just solving for today; you’re creating the foundation for whatever comes next. This directly implements your technical principles around simplicity, maintainability, and evolution.

选那种不会让未来的你咒骂过去的你的技术。选技术就像纹身：它会陪你很长时间，或者要花大价钱才能洗掉，所以请明智选择。我们已经讨论过“选择无聊技术”、不追新鲜玩意儿，但值得再强调一次。问问自己：“这能解决我们的真实问题吗？”以及“当当初倡导它的人不可避免地离开后，我们还能维护它吗？”记住，你不只是在解决今天的问题，你在为接下来的一切打地基。这直接落地了你关于简洁、可维护性和演进的技术原则。

Risk management (or, expecting the unexpected). Something will go wrong—we promise. The question is whether you’ve thought about what those things might be and how you’ll handle them. You don’t need elaborate contingency plans for every possible scenario (that would be an overengineering red flag). Instead, identify your biggest risks, have a basic plan for each, and ensure everyone knows who is responsible for what when things get tough.

风险管理（或者说，预期到意外）。一定会出问题——我们保证。问题在于，你有没有想过可能是哪些事、以及你会怎么应对。你不需要为每一种可能场景都准备精细的应急预案（那会是过度设计的危险信号）。相反，识别你最大的几个风险，为每个风险准备一份基本计划，并确保每个人都清楚：当事情变糟时，谁负责什么。

Regularly check in on your risks—new ones always pop up, especially in chaotic environments. Yesterday’s “unlikely” might be today’s “oh crap, that’s happening right now.”

定期复盘你的风险——新的风险总会冒出来，尤其是在混乱环境里。昨天的“不太可能”，可能就是今天的“我靠，这事正在发生”。

“But that’s not what I meant!” Miscommunication and assumptions are the common sources of failure in technical programs. People use the same words to mean completely different things. What’s “done” to an engineer might be “ready for testing” to a product manager and “ready to ship” to a customer success person. Or they make assumptions because something isn’t transparent to them.

“可我不是这个意思！”沟通不畅和主观假设，是技术项目失败的常见根源。人们用同样的词表达完全不同的意思。对工程师来说“完成”的东西，对产品经理可能是“可以测试了”，对客户成功可能是“可以发布了”。又或者，因为某件事对他们不透明，他们就自行假设。

Create a shared language. Write things down. Have regular check-ins where people can ask “stupid” questions (spoiler: there really are no stupid questions). Document decisions and the reasoning behind them. The future you will thank you when remembering why you chose that particular approach six months ago. This imple‐ments your documentation principle in practice.

创造一门共享语言。把事情写下来。定期开这样的碰头会：大家可以问“蠢问题”（剧透：真的没有蠢问题）。把决策及其背后的理由文档化。六个月后，当你回想当初为什么选那个方案时，未来的你会感谢现在的你。这在实践中落地了你的文档化原则。

— 原书第 188 页 —

Keeping your finger on the pulse. We cannot emphasize enough that your strategy is a living thing, not a fossil. Set up simple ways to monitor how things are going. This could include dashboards, regular check-ins, or asking the right questions during your standups. The point is to know whether your brilliant plan is actually working before it’s too late to make a course correction.

把手指放在脉搏上。我们再怎么强调都不为过：你的战略是活的东西，不是化石。建立简单的方式来监控进展。可以是仪表盘、定期复盘，或在站会上问对的问题。关键是：在还来得及纠偏之前，就知道你那套聪明计划到底有没有真的奏效。

Look for both technical metrics (e.g., “Is the system performing better?”) and human ones (e.g., “Is the team less stressed? Are we shipping faster?”). Both matter. This directly implements your “visibility matters” principle.

既要看技术指标（例如“系统性能更好了吗？”），也要看人的指标（例如“团队压力小了吗？我们交付更快了吗？”）。两者都重要。这直接落地了你“可观测性很重要”的原则。

We cover metrics in more detail in Chapter 10.

我们会在第 10 章更详细地讨论指标。

Balancing all the things. Remember the trade-off discussion from earlier? Every technical decision involves them. Be explicit about what you’re prioritizing and why. It’s okay to say, “We’re choosing this approach because speed to market is more important than perfect scalability right now.” Just make sure everyone understands the trade-offs you’re making. It’s important that you document these decisions, as they embody your principles in action.

在所有事情之间找平衡。还记得前面关于权衡的讨论吗？每个技术决策都包含权衡。明确说清楚你在优先什么、以及为什么。你完全可以说：“我们选这个方案，是因为眼下上市速度比完美的可扩展性更重要。”只要确保每个人都理解你在做什么权衡。把这些决策文档化很重要，因为它们就是你的原则在行动中的化身。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April faced a classic trade-off in the StudioOps team: the animation rendering engine needed optimization for 4K displays (customer request), but the authentication system needed security updates (compliance requirement). She made the trade-off explicit in a team meeting: “We can do 4K support in Q1 and security in Q2, risking a compliance audit failure, or we can do security first but potentially lose our biggest customer who needs 4K by March.” The team discussed and decided on a hybrid: implement the critical security patches in two sprints (not the full rewrite), then focus on 4K, and then return to complete the security overhaul. April documented this decision in their architecture decision record: “We chose tactical security fixes over a complete authentication overhaul to balance compliance risk against customer retention. The full overhaul is scheduled for Q2 after the 4K feature ships.”

April 在 StudioOps 团队遇到了一个经典权衡：动画渲染引擎需要为 4K 显示做优化（客户要求），但认证系统需要安全更新（合规要求）。她在团队会议上把这个权衡摆上台面：“我们可以 Q1 做 4K 支持、Q2 做安全，但要冒合规审计失败的风险；或者先做安全，但可能丢掉那个三月就需要 4K 的最大客户。”团队讨论后决定走混合路线：用两个 sprint 实现关键安全补丁（而不是整体重写），然后专注做 4K，之后再回头完成安全大整改。April 把这个决策写进了他们的架构决策记录（ADR）：“我们选择战术性安全修复而非彻底的认证整改，以在合规风险与客户留存之间取得平衡。完整整改计划在 Q2、4K 功能上线之后进行。”

— 原书第 189 页 —

Building capabilities, not just systems. Implementing new technologies often requires new skills. Ensure your team has the necessary training and support in place. This isn’t just about formal training; it’s about creating space for people to learn, experiment, and build confidence with new approaches.

建设能力，而不只是系统。落地新技术往往需要新技能。确保团队有必要的培训和支持。这不只是正式培训，更是为人们创造空间，让他们去学习、试验，并在新方法上建立信心。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

When April standardized StudioOps on PostgreSQL, she didn’t just mandate the change; she set up “PostgreSQL Fridays” where Derek (who knows PostgreSQL well) ran hands‐on sessions. This included topics like “basic query optimization” in week 1, “JSON functions for document storage” in week 2, and “full-text search configuration” in week 3. She also purchased a team license for a PostgreSQL performance course and allocated four hours per week for learning. The initial productivity dip was real—feature velocity dropped 30% in the first month. But by month two, the team was shipping faster than before because they weren’t constantly context switching between database paradigms. The juniors especially benefited; instead of being confused by five different query lan‐guages, they could actually become proficient in one.

当 April 把 StudioOps 标准化到 PostgreSQL 时，她不只是下命令推行变更，还设立了“PostgreSQL 星期五”，由 Derek（精通 PostgreSQL）主持实操环节。内容包括第 1 周“基础查询优化”、第 2 周“用于文档存储的 JSON 函数”、第 3 周“全文检索配置”。她还为团队买了一门 PostgreSQL 性能课程的授权，每周划出四小时用于学习。初期的生产力下滑是真实的——第一个月功能交付速度下降了 30%。但到第二个月，团队交付得比以前更快了，因为他们不再在五种数据库范式之间频繁切换上下文。初级工程师尤其受益：他们不再被五种不同的查询语言搞得晕头转向，而是真的能精通其中一种。

Be patient. Learning takes time, and productivity often dips before it improves when people adapt to new ways of working. That’s normal and expected, not a sign of failure.

要有耐心。学习需要时间；当人们适应新的工作方式时，生产力往往会先下滑再提升。这是正常且预期之中的，不是失败的信号。

Communicating the vision. People need to understand what they’re doing and why it matters. Help them by connecting the dots between individual work and the larger technical and business goals. Repeat the message more than necessary in every available medium; people need to hear something multiple times before it sinks in, and everyone consumes information differently.

沟通愿景。人们需要理解自己在做什么、以及它为什么重要。帮他们把个人工作与更宏大的技术和业务目标连成线。在一切可用的媒介上，把信息重复到超过必要的程度；人们要把一件事听上很多遍才能真正听进去，而且每个人接收信息的方式都不同。

And make it concrete. “We’re improving system reliability” is vague. But “We’re reducing customer-facing errors by 50% so people can complete their purchases without frustration” gives people something tangible to rally around. Your team should be able to understand the mission, know how it is being measured, and explain how it is happening, when it is happening, and what their involvement or ownership is.

而且要具体。“我们在提升系统可靠性”是模糊的；但“我们要把面向客户的错误减少 50%，让人们能毫无挫败地完成购买”，给了大家一个可以围绕它凝聚共识的具体东西。你的团队应当能理解使命、知道它如何被度量，并能解释：它是怎么发生的、什么时候发生、以及他们自己的参与或负责的部分是什么。

— 原书第 190 页 —

Leading by example. Leaders play a crucial role in sustaining improvement. If you’re in a leadership position, you need to champion the strategy visibly and show that you’re open to feedback and adaptation. Nothing kills a strategy faster than leaders who say, “This is important,” but then ignore it in their actions.

以身作则。领导者在维持改进方面扮演关键角色。如果你身处领导岗位，你需要可见地为战略站台，并表现出你对反馈和调整持开放态度。没有什么比这种领导更快扼杀战略了：嘴上说“这件事很重要”，行动上却无视它。

Celebrate wins, learn from setbacks, and connect the technical work to the larger mission. Help people see how their daily efforts contribute to the bigger picture. The most potent form of communication isn’t what you say; it’s what you do. Leaders need to model the behaviors they want to see: embracing change, being open to feedback, and focusing on outcomes rather than perfect adherence to a plan.

庆祝胜利、从挫折中学习，并把技术工作连接到更宏大的使命上。帮人们看到自己的日常努力如何贡献于大局。最有力的沟通形式不是你说了什么，而是你做了什么。领导者需要以身作则地示范自己希望看到的行为：拥抱变化、对反馈开放、聚焦于结果而不是完美地死守计划。

If you say “learning from failure is important” but then publicly roast the first person whose project doesn’t go as planned, guess what message people are actually hearing? Your actions always speak louder than your words. You must embody the technical principles you’ve established.

如果你嘴上说“从失败中学习很重要”，转头却公开痛批第一个项目没按计划走的人，猜猜人们实际听到的是什么信息？你的行动永远比你的话更响亮。你必须亲身践行自己确立的技术原则。

Conclusion: Enabling Execution with Technical Strategy

结语：用技术战略赋能执行

A good technical strategy aligns your decisions with your goals, strikes a balance between innovation and practicality, and sets you up for sustainable growth. It’s not about creating the perfect plan but establishing a clear direction and approach that can evolve as conditions change.

一套好的技术战略，让你的决策与目标对齐，在创新与务实之间取得平衡，并为可持续增长打好基础。它不在于造出完美的计划，而在于确立一个清晰的方向和路径，并能随条件变化而演进。

The most successful strategies embrace the reality of change rather than trying to predict every detail up front. By building flexibility and learning into your approach, you become better equipped to navigate challenges.

最成功的战略拥抱变化的现实，而不是试图预先预测每一个细节。通过把灵活性和学习能力建进你的方法里，你会更有能力驾驭挑战。

Remember, at its heart, technical strategy is about enabling your organization to succeed, not just deploying cool technology. Keep your focus on the outcomes you’re trying to achieve, be thoughtful about the trade-offs you’re making, and bring your people along on the journey.

记住：从根本上说，技术战略是为了让组织成功，而不只是部署酷的技术。把焦点放在你想达成的结果上，用心权衡你所做的取舍，并让你的人和你一起走完这段旅程。

With a solid but adaptable strategy, you’ll be better positioned to tackle the chaos, seize opportunities as they emerge, and build systems that can grow and evolve with your business.

有一套扎实但可适应的战略，你就能更好地应对混乱、在机会出现时抓住它们，并构建能与业务一起成长、一起演进的系统。

In Chapter 9, we’ll talk about how to take your strategy and turn it into technical practices.

在第 9 章，我们会讨论如何把你的战略转化为技术实践。
